title: Remove While Iterating, Without ConcurrentModificationException
statement:
A `for`-each loop over a `List` is sugar for calling `iterator()` once
and driving it by hand -- and that iterator keeps its own count of how
many structural changes (adds or removes) the list has been through since
it was created. Call `list.remove(...)` directly, mid-loop, and the
iterator's count falls out of step with the list's own: the very next
`hasNext()`/`next()` call notices the mismatch and throws
`ConcurrentModificationException` -- Java's collections *fail fast* on
this rather than silently producing a wrong answer.

## Your function

```
public static void removeMultiplesOf(List<Integer> values, int n);
```

`n` is always at least `1`. **Mutate `values` in place**, removing every
element that is a multiple of `n` (including `0`, a multiple of
everything), and keeping the relative order of everything that survives.
`values` may be empty.

## Watch out

- **`for (Integer v : values) { if (v % n == 0) values.remove(v); }`
  throws `ConcurrentModificationException` on the very first removal it
  makes**, not just on some of them -- the for-each loop's implicit
  iterator has already advanced past the point a direct list mutation
  invalidates, and the exception fires the next time the loop asks the
  iterator for anything at all, which is almost always the very next
  iteration (or the loop's own final check that there is nothing left).
- **`values.removeIf(predicate)` is built for exactly this and does the
  whole job in one call**, safely: it is implemented to remove matching
  elements without leaving any externally-visible iterator in an invalid
  state, because there never is one -- there is nothing for a candidate
  to get wrong here beyond writing the right predicate.
- **An explicit `Iterator<Integer>`, calling *its own* `remove()` method,
  is the one form of "remove while iterating" Java actually allows.**
  `Iterator.remove()` updates the iterator's own bookkeeping as part of
  removing, which is precisely what a direct `list.remove(...)` call does
  not do -- the same underlying operation, safe through one path and not
  through the other, depending on which object's `remove()` you call.

tests.name: no multiples present -- nothing is removed
every element is a multiple -- the result is empty
a single match in the middle throws for the naive for-each version
tests.description: Only one element (3) matches -- a for-each loop calling list.remove() directly throws ConcurrentModificationException on this alone, not just on multiple removals.

tests.name: only the last element matches
tests.description: Even a removal that happens to be the last element in the list still throws for the naive version -- there is no safe position for the bug to hide in.

tests.name: zero is a multiple of everything
